summary:
SeloAI helps US farmers plan crop rotations that hold up as the climate changes. A farmer picks a real field on a map of USDA field boundaries in the Corn Belt. They choose what matters most to them, and SeloAI answers three questions. Which crop fits this field next year? When during the year is the field vulnerable to bare soil, drought, heat, frost or heavy rain? Which 3-year rotations would make it more resilient than the current one?

SeloAI combines 8 years of field crop history (USDA Crop Sequence Boundaries) with daily NASA POWER weather, NASADEM terrain and SSURGO soil data. Agronomic rules and a machine-learning model trained on 12,869 field seasons process them. Each strategy shows numbers (erosion, bare-soil days, water use, nitrogen balance, income), plain-language reasons, data gaps and what to check with an agronomist. Farmers can save and compare fields and download a PDF report.

Rotation choices decide soil loss, water stress and income, yet NASA data rarely reaches farmers in a usable form. SeloAI turns it into clear options. It supports the farmer's decision; it does not replace it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SeloAI is a web app for crop-rotation decisions on real US fields in Iowa, Illinois and Nebraska. A farmer finds a field on the map, by county or township, or by pasting coordinates or a Google/Apple Maps link. The field outline comes from USDA Crop Sequence Boundaries, which also give 8 years of crop history (2018-2025). The farmer picks priorities (for example soil health, water or income), a planning horizon and, optionally, their own costs.

SeloAI then returns:

- a ranking of crops for next year, with probabilities and reasons;

- a 12-month vulnerability timeline: bare soil, drought, heat, frost and heavy rain;

- the current rotation plus 3 alternative 3-year rotations built on different logic. Each shows erosion, bare-soil days, water use, nitrogen balance and an income index, with the difference from the current rotation;

- for every strategy, the risks, the data behind it, the data gaps, and what to check with a local agronomist.

Farmers can save fields, compare them side by side, rank fields in a county or township, and estimate profit per acre from university extension budgets. They can also download a PDF report to share with an agronomist, landlord or lender.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: daily NASA POWER weather 2017-2025 (growing degree days, heat and frost days, dry spells, heavy rain, water balance), NASADEM slope processed in Google Earth Engine, USDA SSURGO soil (clay, organic matter, pH, salinity, water capacity, drainage, erodibility) and crop history. Landsat/HLS NDVI and SMAP soil moisture pipelines are being added.

2. 53 features per field and year, using only what a farmer knows before sowing. The weather of the coming season is never used, so there is no hidden leakage.

3. Agronomic rules remove crops that should not follow the previous one. Suitability ranges score how well soil and climate fit each crop. A LightGBM model, trained on 12,869 field seasons from 1,994 fields in Iowa, Illinois, Nebraska and Kansas, gives calibrated probabilities.

4. An agronomic calculator (FAO-56 water use, simplified RUSLE erosion, nitrogen fixation, bare days) scores each rotation.

Results: tested on fields the model never saw, it picks the right crop 78.2% of the time, against 66.7% for simple corn-soybean alternation. The right crop is in its top 3 in 98.8% of cases. In Kansas, where rotations are less regular, it is right 67% of the time against 35% for alternation. Probabilities are calibrated: when it says 85%, it is right about 85% of the time.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Rotation choices decide soil loss, water stress and income. Example, Polk County, Iowa: adding a winter cereal rye cover crop to corn-soybean cuts bare-soil days from 189 to 74 per year and halves modeled erosion (8.9 to 4.4 t/ha). The trade-off is more water use and a slightly lower income index; the farmer decides. The tool is also honest when change is not worth it: on a dry western Nebraska wheat-fallow field, no alternative scores clearly better, and all need 2.5-3.7 times more water. Our aim is to make free NASA Earth data useful at the scale of one field and one decision, for farmers with no remote-sensing skills.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, PMTiles vector tiles, TanStack Query, Feature-Sliced Design; Vitest, Playwright and MSW for tests.

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, PostgreSQL + PostGIS, GeoPandas/Shapely, tippecanoe, WeasyPrint + Jinja2 for PDF reports, Argon2 + JWT auth. An OpenAPI contract is checked automatically against real responses.

- ML: Python, LightGBM, pandas, NumPy, Google Earth Engine.

- Infrastructure: Docker, GitHub Actions CI, Heroku, Neon (Postgres), Vercel. No special hardware: everything ran on our laptops and free or low-cost cloud tiers.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It plans rotations over several years, not single crops, and always compares them with what the farmer grows today.

- It speaks farmer language: townships, map links, plain wording instead of model jargon.

- It shows its uncertainty: calibrated probabilities, named data gaps, and checks to do with an agronomist.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Trust: every number has a source, missing data is reported, not guessed, and the tool supports the farmer's decision rather than replacing it.

- Scientific honesty: validation on unseen fields, comparison with a simple baseline, and agronomic limits checked against real plantings (99-100% of real fields fall inside them).

- Coarse data: POWER (~50 km) and SMAP (~11 km) describe the region, not the single field, and we say so.

- Economics: costs and prices change income figures but never change the agronomic ranking. Unknown costs stay unknown.

- Privacy and access: accounts are only needed to save fields and estimate profit; analysis works without sign-in.
